(a) Section 147 of the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011 (Public Law 111–242), as added by section 1(a)(2) of the Continuing Appropriations and Surface Transportation Extensions Act, 2011 (Public Law 111–322; 5 U.S.C. 5303 note), is amended—
        (1) in subsection (b)(1), by striking the matter after “ending on” and before “shall be made” and inserting “December 31, 2013,”; and 
        (2) in subsection (c), by striking the matter after “ending on” and before “no senior executive” and inserting “December 31, 2013,”.  
    (b) Section 114 of the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2013 (Public Law 112–175; 5 U.S.C. 5303 note) is repealed.

fable.w: This section only amends dates in an earlier appropriations provision on federal pay adjustments and repeals another provision. There is no tempting reading here: it involves no consultation, hearing, comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue for any party outside the federal government.
fable.s: by striking the matter after “ending on” and before “shall be made” and inserting “December 31, 2013,”

qwen_block.w: This section consists entirely of technical amendments to existing statutes, specifically changing dates and repealing a previous section. It does not establish any process for consultation, public comment, advisory boards, or coordination with outside parties. The text deals solely with internal legislative housekeeping and statutory dates.
qwen_block.s: (a) Section 147 of the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011 ... is amended— (1) in subsection (b)(1), by striking the matter after “ending on” and before “shall be made” and inserting “December 31, 2013,”; and (2) in subsection (c), by striking the matter after “ending on” and before “no senior executive” and inserting “December 31, 2013,”. (b) Section 114 of the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2013 ... is repealed.

opus.w: The section changes end dates in a prior appropriations act to December 31, 2013, and repeals Section 114 of the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2013. It creates no comment period, rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to sue. Mentioning federal pay and senior executives does not bring any outside party into a federal decision.
opus.b: The tempting reading would be to treat this as an agency decision because it touches federal pay rules (5 U.S.C. 5303 note) and senior executive pay. That reading fails. The section only changes an end date to "December 31, 2013" and repeals a section. No one outside the federal government takes part in any decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the expiration dates of salary freeze provisions for federal employees and repeals a previous section. It involves only internal legislative changes and federal employees. There is no requirement for consultation with, or participation by, any party outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities). The text contains no mechanisms for public comment, hearings, or advisory committees involving non-federal members.
qwen_chat.s: (a) Section 147 of the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011 (Public Law 111–242), as added by section 1(a)(2) of the Continuing Appropriations and Surface Transportation Extensions Act, 2011 (Public Law 111–322; 5 U.S.C. 5303 note), is amended— (1) in subsection (b)(1), by striking the matter after “ending on” and before “shall be made” and inserting “December 31, 2013,”; and (2) in subsection (c), by striking the matter after “ending on” and before “no senior executive” and inserting “December 31, 2013,”. (b) Section 114 of the Continuing Appropriations Resolution, 2013 (Public Law 112–175; 5 U.S.C. 5303 note) is repealed.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that amending dates in appropriations acts involves some form of procedural change that could imply consultation, but the text itself is purely technical, dealing with the expiration of salary freeze provisions. There is no mention of any outside party, public comment, hearing, or advisory committee. The actors involved are Congress (via the statute itself) and federal employees (whose salaries are affected). Since Congress is inside the federal government and the text does not grant any right to outsiders to participate in the decision-making process, this is not participation.
